Belgian Economic Activity Rebounds as Political Crisis Ends

Belgian businesses are resuming normal operations after the country emerged from a weeklong government crisis that had disrupted economic activity nationwide. The crisis, triggered by the abrupt resignation of Prime Minister Claire Marchand amid allegations of foreign interference, led to widespread uncertainty and delays in key administrative processes, affecting both domestic and international companies.

Umicore SA, one of Belgium’s largest materials technology firms, confirmed that its production facilities, which had experienced slowdowns due to customs processing delays and disrupted supply chains, have returned to normal output as of Tuesday. “The government’s swift resolution of the political impasse has allowed us to restart all affected operations,” said an Umicore spokesperson. “We are working closely with our partners to address any remaining backlogs.”

The crisis began when the federal coalition government collapsed over allegations that a non-EU country had exerted pressure on Belgian decision-makers regarding trade policy. As a result, the temporary caretaker government paused the issuance of certain export permits and enhanced border checks, causing delays for manufacturers and exporters.

According to the Belgian Federation of Enterprises, the disruptions cost the economy an estimated €140 million in lost output, as shipments were held at ports and paperwork accumulated. “The uncertainty was especially challenging for companies dependent on just-in-time delivery,” noted Bernard De Smet, chief economist at the federation.

The caretaker government and opposition leaders reached a consensus late Sunday to form an interim cabinet and restore administrative functions. Customs and border agents were instructed to clear the backlog as a top priority.

Workers’ unions have welcomed the resolution but urged policymakers to reinforce safeguards against foreign influence. “Belgium’s economic stability depends on strong, resilient institutions,” said Marie Lemaire, spokesperson for the General Workers Union.
